visuals.label: Tax point, returns and records
rows: The basic tax point for goods
The time the goods are removed, or the time they are made available to the person supplied.
The basic tax point for services
When the services are performed.
Payment or invoice first
If the supplier issues a VAT invoice or receives payment BEFORE the goods are delivered or made available, the tax point is brought forward to that earlier date.
Invoice within 14 days after
If a VAT invoice is issued within 14 days after the basic tax point, the invoice date becomes the new tax point.
The return
An electronic return each quarter, due 1 month and 7 days after the end of the VAT period. Payment is due on the same deadline, by direct debit.
Why the quarters differ
Businesses are allocated four different VAT periods across the year so that HMRC receives an even distribution of VAT during the year.
The invoice

A taxable person supplying another taxable person must give a tax invoice showing the VAT number, the tax point, the value of the supply and the rate charged. Invoices are issued to all customers regardless of their VAT status.
The records

Records of all taxable goods and services received or supplied, including exempt supplies made — annual accounts, bank statements, purchase and sale invoices, daily takings and relevant correspondence — plus a VAT account summarising input and output VAT for each period. No prescribed format, but HMRC must be able to check the return from it.

visuals.label: The figures to memorise, and the penalties
cols: THE POSITION FOR 6 APRIL 2026 TO 5 APRIL 2027
rows: Compulsory registration threshold
£90,000 of taxable supplies. The same as the previous tax year.
Deregistration threshold
£88,000. The same as the previous tax year.
The rates
Standard 20%, reduced 5%, zero 0%. The same as the previous tax year.
The VAT fraction
For a standard rated supply the VAT element of a VAT-inclusive figure is 1/6, so £120 inclusive contains £20 of VAT. For a reduced rate supply the fraction is 1/21, so £105 inclusive contains £5.
Failure to register
A penalty of a percentage of the VAT due from the date registration should have happened. The percentage rises the longer the delay.
Late return or late payment
A percentage surcharge on the VAT due, rising to a maximum of 15% for consistent defaults.
Under-declaring the VAT due
A penalty as a percentage of the tax that should have been paid, where the under-declaration is due to significant or repeated lack of care.
Dishonest evasion
A penalty of up to the amount of VAT evaded, and evasion can also lead to an unlimited fine and imprisonment for up to 7 years.

notes.head: 7.19.2 What counts as a supply
body: Any transfer of the whole property in goods is a supply of GOODS. That covers consumer goods, but also the supply of power or heat, the grant of an interest in land, and a GIFT of goods.
Anything that is not a supply of goods is a supply of SERVICES if it is provided for consideration — including a lawyer's services for a fee.
The value of the supply is defined widely, to prevent VAT avoidance.
HMRC issues each registering person a VAT number, which is used for all the businesses that person operates.

notes.head: 7.19.3 Registration, and why a new business might volunteer
body: Registration is compulsory once the previous 12 months' taxable supplies exceed the threshold, tested at the end of each month, or once there are reasonable grounds to believe the next 30 days alone will exceed it.

Voluntary registration lets a business recover input tax before it is anywhere near the threshold. A new consultancy charging £10,000 of output tax while paying £20,000 of input tax reclaims £10,000 from HMRC.
The price is that it must charge output tax on everything it supplies, which is a real additional cost to a customer who is not registered and cannot recover it.

notes.head: 7.19.5 The option to tax, in practice
body: The option is available for COMMERCIAL land and buildings only.
Once exercised it applies to all future supplies of that land or building, including selling it and letting it to a tenant.

It relates to that individual property, not to everything the person owns — but within that property it applies to the WHOLE building, which is a problem where several tenants occupy it and some make exempt supplies.
It is made by the owner and does not transfer with the land on a future disposal.
Where the freehold of a commercial building less than 3 years old is sold, the supply is standard rated in any event, without any option.

notes.head: 7.19.6 Why the compliance burden matters
body: The administrative requirements are themselves a disadvantage of being registered, and the SRA specification tests returns, payment and record keeping as well as the charge itself.
The tax point decides which accounting period a supply falls into, which is what makes it worth memorising the four tax point rules.
The penalties are all percentage-based except dishonest evasion, which can reach the whole amount evaded, an unlimited fine and 7 years' imprisonment.

notes.head: CURRENCY
body: The 2026 manual moved the thresholds and rates out of the chapter into the separate Tax Checker, and the March 2026 business update confirms the Tax Checker governs for 7.16 to 7.19. The figures here come from the Tax Checker of 24 July 2026.

The 3-year rule for a new commercial building is kept although the 2026 chapter does not spell it out, because it is accurate law and the chapter's own example — a landlord buying a new commercial building and paying standard rate VAT on it — only makes sense with it.

statutes.text: VAT is charged on any supply of goods or services made in the United Kingdom where it is a taxable supply made by a taxable person in the course or furtherance of any business carried on by them. A taxable supply is any supply other than an exempt supply.

Lists the zero-rated groups, including food other than that supplied in the course of catering, water and sewerage services, books and newspapers, transport and the construction of residential buildings.
Lists the exempt groups, including land, insurance, financial services, postal services, education, health and welfare, and burial and cremation.
Contains the option to tax. It permits the owner of an interest in commercial land or buildings to elect to waive the exemption, and sets out the conditions for revoking that option.

7.19.tip: ⚡ SQE: The four treatments are STANDARD 20%, REDUCED 5%, ZERO 0% and EXEMPT — and zero rated is a TAXABLE supply, so input tax is recoverable, while exempt is not, so it is not. Outside the scope: private sale, MOT fee, sale of shares, business sold as a going concern. Register when the previous 12 months exceed £90,000 (rolling monthly test) or the next 30 days alone will; deregister below £88,000. Land is normally exempt; the owner of COMMERCIAL property may opt to tax to unlock input tax recovery, and that option covers the whole building, binds all future supplies, and can only be revoked within 6 months or after 20 years. Returns quarterly, 1 month and 7 days after the period end. Input tax on cars and on business entertaining is blocked.

7.20.title: Inheritance Tax

visuals.label: Mind map — the whole of 7.20

branches.label: WHAT BUSINESS RELIEF DOES
leaves: Business relief reduces the taxable VALUE of business property, whether it is given away in the donor's lifetime or passes on death
It is given AUTOMATICALLY once the conditions are met — there is no formal claim to make
The relief is either 100% or 50%, depending on the asset and on how much tax-free giving the donor has already used
The 2026 manual renamed it: what used to be called BUSINESS PROPERTY RELIEF (BPR) is now simply BUSINESS RELIEF (BR)

branches.label: WHAT GETS 100% RELIEF
leaves: A SOLE TRADER BUSINESS
An INTEREST IN A PARTNERSHIP
UNQUOTED SHARES — shares in a company not listed on a recognised stock exchange
The 100% rate applies only up to £2.5m of qualifying transfers in any rolling 7-year period. Anything above that threshold drops to 50%

branches.label: WHAT GETS ONLY 50% RELIEF
leaves: Shares listed on the ALTERNATIVE INVESTMENT MARKET, however small their value
Shares in a QUOTED company where the donor has VOTING CONTROL
LAND, BUILDINGS, PLANT OR MACHINERY owned personally by the donor but used by a partnership they belong to, or by a company they control
Any qualifying transfer above the £2.5m rolling threshold
Quoted company shares where the donor does NOT have voting control are not qualifying assets at all and get nothing

branches.label: THE THREE CONDITIONS
leaves: The business must be TRADING — a business that holds or makes investments, or deals in land and property, is excluded
The donor must have OWNED the business property for at least 2 YEARS before the transfer
The company must not be stuffed with EXCEPTED ASSETS, or the relief is cut proportionately
Shares in an OVERSEAS trading company do qualify — the trading test, not the location, is what matters

branches.label: WHAT HAPPENS AFTERWARDS
leaves: On a gift into a TRUST, a chargeable lifetime transfer, the relief bites immediately and reduces the lifetime tax
On a gift to an INDIVIDUAL, a potentially exempt transfer, there is no immediate tax, so the relief has nothing to reduce yet
If the donor dies within 7 years, the donee must have KEPT the property, or have reinvested ALL the net sale proceeds in other business property
Withdrawal of the relief only affects the tax on DEATH; the original lifetime calculation on a chargeable lifetime transfer is left undisturbed

visuals.label: Decision tree — does Business Relief apply, and at what rate?

nodes.q: 1. Is this a qualifying business asset, and at what rate?

a.k: A SOLE TRADER BUSINESS, A PARTNERSHIP INTEREST, OR UNQUOTED SHARES
a.v: 100% relief, provided the £2.5m rolling threshold has not been exceeded.

a.k: SHARES ON THE ALTERNATIVE INVESTMENT MARKET
a.v: Alternative investment market shares get 50% relief only, even where the value is well below the threshold. The other 50% is treated as a potentially exempt transfer that may later become taxable.

a.k: QUOTED SHARES WHERE THE DONOR HAS VOTING CONTROL
a.v: Quoted shares carrying voting control get 50% relief only.

a.k: LAND, BUILDINGS, PLANT OR MACHINERY OWNED PERSONALLY AND USED BY THE DONOR'S PARTNERSHIP OR CONTROLLED COMPANY
a.v: Land, buildings, plant and machinery owned personally get 50% relief only, because the asset belongs to the individual rather than to the business.
Not a qualifying asset. No relief at all.

nodes.q: 2. Is the business a trading business?

a.v: The condition is met. Trading overseas is fine: shares in overseas trading companies are eligible.

a.k: NO — IT HOLDS OR MAKES INVESTMENTS
a.v: Excluded. No relief.

a.k: NO — IT DEALS IN LAND OR PROPERTY
a.v: Excluded. A company buying land and property for rental income, or to sell on once it has appreciated, is dealing in land and gets nothing.

nodes.q: 3. Has the donor owned the property for 2 years?

a.v: The ownership condition is met.

a.k: NO, BUT IT REPLACED AN EARLIER BUSINESS ASSET
a.v: Still eligible, so long as the two periods of ownership together come to 2 years.

a.k: NO, BUT IT WAS INHERITED FROM A SPOUSE OR CIVIL PARTNER ON DEATH
a.v: Still eligible. The survivor is automatically credited with the deceased's ownership period, so the property is treated as acquired on the date the deceased first acquired it.
No relief, however plainly the asset qualifies in every other respect.

nodes.q: 4. Does the company hold excepted assets?

a.v: One that was neither used for business purposes throughout the 2 years before the transfer, nor is required for future use in the business.
Shares or securities held for investment, assets held for the personal use of the transferor or someone connected with them, and large cash deposits not needed in the business.
The relief is cut in proportion. If 30% of the company's net assets are excepted, only 70% relief is given and 30% of the transfer is taxable.

visuals.label: Decision tree — does the relief survive the donor's death?

nodes.q: Was the gift into a trust, or to an individual?

a.k: INTO A TRUST — A CHARGEABLE LIFETIME TRANSFER
a.v: The relief reduced the transfer of value when the lifetime tax was worked out. That calculation stands. Even if the donor dies within 7 years, no further tax is levied on that transfer.

a.k: TO AN INDIVIDUAL — A POTENTIALLY EXEMPT TRANSFER
a.v: Nothing was chargeable at the time, so the relief had nothing to reduce. Whether it is available on death depends on what the donee did with the property.

nodes.q: The gift was to an individual and the donor has died within 7 years. What did the donee do with it?

a.k: KEPT THE BUSINESS PROPERTY UNTIL THE DONOR'S DEATH
a.v: The relief is available.

a.k: SOLD IT AND REINVESTED THE WHOLE OF THE NET PROCEEDS IN OTHER BUSINESS PROPERTY
a.v: The relief is available. The replacement need not be the same kind of business property as the original.

a.k: REINVESTED ONLY PART OF THE PROCEEDS
a.v: No relief. This is an all-or-nothing provision — there is no partial relief for a partial reinvestment.

a.k: SOLD IT AND KEPT THE MONEY
a.v: The relief is withdrawn and the transfer is 100% taxable, subject to any other exemption, relief or the nil rate band.

visuals.label: The rates side by side
rows: A sole trader business
Only up to £2.5m of qualifying transfers in a rolling 7-year period. Above that, 50%.
An interest in a partnership
Same threshold. Agricultural disposals count towards the same total.
Unquoted shares in a trading company
Same threshold, and the relief is cut proportionately for excepted assets.
Shares on the alternative investment market
50% regardless of value. The unrelieved half is a potentially exempt transfer.
Quoted shares where the donor has voting control
Voting control is what brings them in at all.
Quoted shares without voting control
Nothing
Not a qualifying asset.
Land, buildings, plant or machinery owned personally and used by the donor's partnership or controlled company
The asset is owned by the individual, not the business — that is why it is halved.

visuals.label: The inheritance tax framework this relief sits inside

branches.label: THE NIL RATE BANDS
leaves: The NIL RATE BAND is £325,000. Value within it is taxed at 0%, and value above it at 40%
The RESIDENCE NIL RATE BAND adds £175,000 where a qualifying residential interest passes to DIRECT DESCENDANTS — children and grandchildren, not siblings or parents
Both are frozen until APRIL 2031, along with the £2m residence nil rate band taper threshold
Unused nil rate band and residence nil rate band pass to a surviving spouse or civil partner, so a couple can shelter up to £1,000,000
The rate drops from 40% to 36% where at least 10% of the net estate goes to charity

branches.label: LIFETIME GIFTS
leaves: A POTENTIALLY EXEMPT TRANSFER is a gift to an individual. It is fully exempt if the donor survives 7 years, and chargeable if they do not
A CHARGEABLE LIFETIME TRANSFER is a gift into a trust. It is charged at 20% straight away, and topped up towards 40% if the donor dies within 7 years
CUMULATION: chargeable transfers in the 7 years before death eat into the nil rate band available to the death estate

branches.label: TAPER RELIEF
leaves: Taper relief reduces the TAX PAYABLE on a failed potentially exempt transfer, not the value of the transfer and not the nil rate band it used
Death within 3 years of the gift: the full tax is payable
Between 3 and 4 years: 80% of the tax. Between 4 and 5 years: 60%
Between 5 and 6 years: 40%. Between 6 and 7 years: 20%

notes.head: 7.20.1 What business relief is for
body: Inheritance tax is payable on transfers that reduce the value of the donor's estate and are not otherwise exempted or relieved, whether the transfer is made in the donor's lifetime or on death.
Business relief reduces the taxable value of business property given away in lifetime or transferred on death.
It is given automatically once the conditions are satisfied. There is no requirement to make a formal claim.
The chapter is deliberately narrow: the SRA specification tests business relief, and the manual sends you to the Wills manual for the rest of the inheritance tax system.

notes.head: 7.20.2 The rates, and the rolling threshold
body: Business relief gives 100% for most qualifying business assets, up to £2.5m in any rolling 7-year period.
Any transfer of qualifying business assets above that threshold receives only 50% relief.
Disposals of qualifying AGRICULTURAL assets also count towards the same total when you are checking whether the threshold has been reached.
Alternative investment market shares and quoted shares carrying voting control are capped at 50% however low their value.
Other quoted company shares are not qualifying assets at all and get no relief.

notes.head: 7.20.2.2 Trading businesses only
body: Relief is given only if the business carried on by the sole trader, the partnership or the company is TRADING.
A business that holds or makes investments, or that deals in property, is not eligible.
A company that acquires land and property to earn rental income, or to sell on after it appreciates, is dealing in land and is excluded.
Shares in overseas trading companies ARE eligible.

notes.head: 7.20.2.3 The 2-year ownership rule
body: The general rule is that the donor must have owned the business property for at least 2 years before the transfer.
Replacing one business asset with another is an exception, provided the overall period of ownership comes to 2 years.
Inheriting business property from a spouse or civil partner on death is the other exception: the survivor is automatically credited with the deceased's period of ownership.

Four surveyors set up a partnership 6 months ago from an office one of them bought a month before it began. She dies. Both the business and the office are qualifying assets at 100% and 50%, and both fall within the threshold — but neither gets any relief, because neither was owned for 2 years.

notes.head: 7.20.2.4 Excepted assets
body: Relief on a transfer of shares is proportional where the company holds excepted assets.
An excepted asset is one that is neither used for business purposes throughout the 2 years immediately before the transfer, nor required for future use in the business.
Typical examples are shares or securities held for investment, assets held for the personal use of the transferor or a connected person, and large cash deposits not required in the business.

Jacob transfers unquoted trading company shares worth £600,000 to a trust. The company has £1m of net assets, of which £300,000 is cash agreed with HMRC to be an excepted asset. Because 30% of the assets are excepted, Jacob gets 70% relief and £180,000 is taxable.

notes.head: 7.20.3 and 7.20.4 Lifetime transfers and death
body: For calculating lifetime tax, business relief has immediate effect only for gifts into trusts, because potentially exempt transfers are not immediately chargeable and may never become so.

For relief to be available when tax is calculated on the donor's death, the donee must either have retained the business property until the donor died, or have sold it and replaced it with other business property.
On a replacement, the donee must have reinvested the WHOLE of the net proceeds of sale. There is no partial relief for a partial reinvestment.
A withdrawal of relief affects only the tax payable on death. It does not disturb the original lifetime calculation on a chargeable lifetime transfer.

notes.head: CURRENCY
body: The March 2026 business update confirms that business property relief is now known simply as BUSINESS RELIEF, and directs you to the Tax Checker for current rates.

The £2.5m rolling 7-year threshold and the 50% treatment of alternative investment market shares are new in the 2026 manual. The earlier version of this section wrongly gave alternative investment market shares 100% relief and did not mention the threshold at all.
The nil rate band and residence nil rate band are frozen until APRIL 2031, not 2028 as this section previously said.
From April 2027, an unused discretionary private pension pot will be added to the estate for inheritance tax. Pension pots currently sit outside inheritance tax.

statutes.text: Sets the rates. Nil on the amount within the nil rate band, 40% on the excess, and a reduced rate of 36% where at least 10% of the net estate is given to charity.
Business relief. Reduces the value transferred by 100% or 50% where the transfer is of relevant business property.
Defines relevant business property, and excludes a business consisting wholly or mainly of dealing in securities, stocks or shares, dealing in land or buildings, or making or holding investments.
The minimum period of ownership. The property must have been owned by the transferor throughout the 2 years immediately before the transfer.

Excepted assets. The value attributable to an asset neither used wholly or mainly for business purposes throughout the 2 years before the transfer, nor required for future use in the business, is left out of the relief.
Transfers within 7 years before death. Relief is only available if the donee retained the original property, or replaced it with qualifying replacement property, until the donor's death.

7.20.tip: ⚡ SQE: Business relief (no longer called business property relief) is AUTOMATIC — there is no claim to make. 100% covers a sole trader business, a partnership interest and UNQUOTED shares, up to £2.5m of qualifying transfers in a rolling 7 years, and 50% above that. 50% covers AIM shares, quoted shares where the donor has VOTING CONTROL, and land, buildings, plant or machinery owned personally but used by the donor's partnership or controlled company. Quoted shares without control get NOTHING. Three conditions must all hold: the business must TRADE, the donor must have OWNED it for 2 years, and excepted assets cut the relief proportionately. On death within 7 years of a lifetime gift, the donee must still HOLD the property or have reinvested ALL the net proceeds — partial reinvestment gets nothing.

13.8.title: Inheritance Tax and Income Tax and Capital Gains Tax for an Estate

visuals.label: Mind map — the whole of 13.8
visuals.centre: 13.8 IHT, INCOME TAX AND CGT FOR AN ESTATE

branches.label: 13.8.2.1-.4 THE BASICS
leaves: IHT is charged on the value transferred by a CHARGEABLE TRANSFER — transfers on death, and certain lifetime transfers.
NIL RATE BAND £325,000 and RESIDENCE NIL RATE BAND £175,000, both FROZEN to April 2031 with the £2m taper threshold. Above that, 40%.
For deaths from 6 April 2025 the test is LONG-TERM UK RESIDENCE — 10 of the last 20 tax years — not domicile.
A long-term resident is chargeable on WORLDWIDE assets. Anyone else is chargeable on UK assets only.
Value every transfer by the LOSS TO THE DONOR, not by the gain to the recipient.

branches.label: 13.8.2.5-.8 LIFETIME TRANSFERS
leaves: EXEMPT — within one of the exemptions, so never chargeable at all.
POTENTIALLY EXEMPT TRANSFER — a gift to another individual. No lifetime charge, chargeable only if the donor dies within 7 YEARS.
CHARGEABLE LIFETIME TRANSFER — anything else. Gifts to trusts and companies, charged at 20% if trustees pay or 25% if the donor pays.
Gifts to CHARITABLE trusts are exempt; gifts to BARE trusts are PETs.
IHT is CUMULATIVE: look back 7 years FROM THE GIFT at GROSS earlier transfers. Only CLTs use up the nil rate band.

branches.label: 13.8.2.10 THE TWO BIG RELIEFS
leaves: BUSINESS RELIEF, formerly business property relief, and AGRICULTURAL RELIEF reduce the value transferred, and are given BEFORE the annual exemption.
From 6 April 2026 a COMBINED £2.5m CAP applies to 100% relief across both, with 50% above it. Unused allowance is transferable between spouses.
100% BUSINESS RELIEF: a sole trade business, a partnership share, and shares in an UNLISTED trading company with no minimum holding.
50% BUSINESS RELIEF: quoted shares where the donor has voting CONTROL, and personally-owned land, buildings, plant or machinery used by the business.
The business must be TRADING — investment or property dealing is excluded. Ownership 2 years, or 7 YEARS' occupation for TENANTED agricultural land.

branches.label: 13.8.2.11-.12 THE DEATH ESTATE
leaves: The deceased is treated as making a chargeable transfer of the NET estate. The ANNUAL EXEMPTION is not available against it.
Reduce the NRB by chargeable transfers in the 7 years before death. Those often use the whole band, so the estate is taxed at 40% throughout.
The rate falls to 36% where 10% OR MORE of the net estate goes to charity, measured on a baseline that IGNORES the residence NRB.
TRANSFERABLE NRB: the unused PERCENTAGE passes to a surviving spouse, claimed by the second executors, capped at one extra band.
RESIDENCE NRB needs a residence CLOSELY INHERITED by lineal descendants, is tapered £1 for every £2 over £2m, and applies to the DEATH ESTATE only.

branches.label: 13.8.2.13-.14 ANTI-AVOIDANCE AND PAYMENT
leaves: GIFTS WITH RESERVATION OF BENEFIT: an asset given away but still enjoyed is treated as still owned at death, at its DEATH value.
No reservation if the donor pays MARKET RENT, or RELEASES the benefit — but a release is itself a PET at that date.
PRE-OWNED ASSET TAX imposes an INCOME TAX charge where the former owner still benefits and the reservation rules do not catch it.
IHT on death is due 6 MONTHS after the end of the month of death. The personal representatives are liable for the free estate.
An INSTALMENT OPTION covers certain land and business interests: 10 equal annual payments, the first on the normal due date.

branches.label: 13.8.3 THE ADMINISTRATION PERIOD
leaves: Finalise the DECEASED'S own income tax to the date of death FIRST, because tax owed at death is a liability of the estate.
PRs pay INCOME TAX at 20% on non-savings income and interest, and 10.75% on dividends from 2026/2027. NO allowances of any kind.
PRs pay CGT at 24% for ALL assets from 6 April 2026, and 32% on carried interest gains.
The ANNUAL EXEMPT AMOUNT runs for the year of death AND THE NEXT TWO TAX YEARS ONLY.
A distribution is NOT a disposal. The beneficiary takes at PROBATE VALUE, whatever the asset is worth on the day of transfer.

visuals.label: Decision tree — 13.8.2.5 classify the lifetime transfer

nodes.q: 1. Is it a transfer of value at all?

a.k: NOT IF IT IS AT ARM'S LENGTH
a.v: No gratuitous intent, and made in an arm's length transaction between unconnected persons, or as might be expected in one [IHTA 1984 s 10].

a.k: NOT IF IT IS FAMILY MAINTENANCE
a.v: Expenditure on maintaining the donor's family, such as a child's school fees [IHTA 1984 s 11].

a.k: OTHERWISE VALUE BY LOSS TO THE DONOR
a.v: By how much the donor's estate was diminished, not what the recipient gained. Losing control of a company can transfer far more than the shares given away.

nodes.q: 2. Who or what is the recipient?

a.v: Unlimited, in lifetime and on death. Only the first £325,000 is exempt where the donor is UK domiciled and the recipient spouse is not.
Exempt without limit. From April 2024 gifts on death to European Economic Area charities are no longer exempt.
No lifetime charge. Chargeable only if the donor dies within 7 years, and the RECIPIENT pays the tax.

a.k: A TRUST OR A COMPANY — A CLT
a.v: Immediately chargeable. But charitable trusts are exempt and bare trusts are PETs, and a transfer to a company for shares or loan stock has no IHT consequence.

nodes.q: 3. CLT only — how much lifetime tax, and who pays?

a.v: Then identify the NRB for the year of transfer.
Deduct GROSS chargeable transfers made in the 7 years BEFORE the gift to find the band remaining. Tax only the excess.
The lifetime rate where the tax comes out of the trust fund.
Higher because the transfer is GROSSED UP: what leaves the donor's estate is the gift plus the tax paid to HMRC.

visuals.label: Decision tree — 13.8.2.9 the donor dies within 7 years

nodes.q: 1. Was the transfer a PET or a CLT?

a.v: It becomes chargeable. Use the NRB and rates in force AT THE DATE OF DEATH. The recipient is liable.
Additional tax at the 40% death rate, charged on the TRUSTEES. Same calculation, with one difference at the end.

nodes.q: 2. How much nil rate band is left for this transfer?

a.k: LOOK BACK FROM THE GIFT, NOT FROM DEATH
a.v: Deduct gross chargeable transfers made in the 7 years BEFORE the transfer in question.
A transfer made more than 7 years before death still reduces the band available to a later gift, even though it is not itself taxed on the death.

nodes.q: 3. Is TAPER RELIEF available?

a.k: IT REDUCES THE TAX, NOT THE TRANSFER
a.v: It does not reduce the value transferred and it does not restore any nil rate band [IHTA 1984 s 7(4)].
0 to 3 years: no relief, so the full tax is payable.
3 to 4 years: 20% relief. 4 to 5: 40%. 5 to 6: 60%. 6 to 7: 80%. So a gift 6 and a half years before death bears only 20% of the tax.

nodes.q: 4. CLT only — credit for the lifetime tax already paid

a.v: The trustees get credit for the lifetime tax, whoever paid it. The difference is the additional tax payable.
Where the lifetime tax exceeds the death tax, the difference is NOT repaid. The additional IHT is simply reduced to zero.

visuals.label: 13.8.2.6 Exemptions and the figures to memorise
rows: Spouse or civil partner
Unlimited, in lifetime and on death. Restricted to the first £325,000 where the donor is UK domiciled and the recipient spouse is not.
UK charities
Exempt without any monetary limit. From April 2024 gifts on death to EEA charities are no longer exempt.
Small gifts
Up to £250 to any one donee in a tax year, with no limit on the number of donees. ALL OR NOTHING: a £300 birthday gift is a transfer of value of the whole £300, not just the £50 excess.
Marriage or civil partnership

£5,000 from a parent, £2,500 from a grandparent, £2,500 between the parties themselves, £1,000 from anyone else. NOT all or nothing, so only the excess is a transfer of value. One exemption per marriage per donor — a father who gives his daughter £5,000 cannot also claim £1,000 for a gift to his son-in-law.
Normal expenditure out of income

No monetary limit. NORMAL means habitual or regular, happening year after year, and the donor must be left with sufficient income to maintain their normal standard of living. Covers regular cash gifts and life assurance or pension premiums paid for another person.
Annual exemption

£3,000 a year, to one person or shared. Set against gifts in CHRONOLOGICAL order within the tax year. Unused exemption carries forward ONE tax year only, and the current year's must be used before the brought-forward one.

visuals.label: 13.8.2.11 Valuing the death estate
rows: General rule
Open market value at the date of death — the price the asset might reasonably be expected to fetch if sold on the open market at that point.
Quoted shares

Do TWO calculations and take the LOWER. The QUARTER-UP rule takes the lowest of the day's spread and adds a quarter of the difference between lowest and highest. The alternative averages the highest and lowest marked bargains of the day, ignoring special prices.
Quoted shares — worked example
Quoted at 150p to 158p, so the spread is 8p and a quarter of it is 2p, giving a quarter-up price of 152p. Bargains at 148p, 151p and 158p average to 153p. Take the lower: 152p.
Related property

Broadly, similar property owned by a spouse or civil partner. If the asset is worth more taking that into account than on a stand-alone basis, it is valued at the higher amount. A building jointly owned by husband and wife and worth £400,000 gives a half share valued at £200,000.
Jointly owned, not spouses

The related property rules do not apply. A brother's half share is valued stand-alone and is worth less than half the whole, because a buyer would not pay 50% for a share with another co-owner. A discount of between 5% and 15% is usual, negotiated with HMRC.
Excluded property
Outside the estate altogether. As well as non-UK assets of a non-long-term resident, this covers reversionary interests under a life interest trust and interests in a discretionary trust.
Liabilities

Deductible from the assets. Mortgages, income tax owed by the deceased and reasonable funeral expenses are allowable. PROBATE COSTS are not deductible, with a limited exception for overseas probate costs.

visuals.label: 13.8.2.11 Nil rate band and residence nil rate band
rows: The two bands
NRB £325,000 and residence NRB £175,000, both frozen until April 2031, along with the £2m residence NRB taper threshold.
Order of deduction
The residence NRB is not set specifically against the house. Like the general NRB it applies to the net estate generally, and it is deducted BEFORE the general NRB.
Transferable NRB — mechanics
A claim is made by the SECOND spouse's executors, not on the first death. The uplift is a PERCENTAGE: 90% unused when the band was £300,000 gives £292,500 against a £325,000 band, not £270,000.
Transferable NRB — limits

The uplifted NRB is used against all IHT arising on death, including tax on PETs and CLTs, but NOT against lifetime tax on CLTs. Where the taxpayer has survived more than one spouse the total additional band is capped at one full NRB, so the maximum anyone can have is twice the band for the year of death.
Residence NRB — three conditions

The estate contains a QUALIFYING RESIDENTIAL INTEREST, a dwelling house used at some point as the deceased's private residence; it is CLOSELY INHERITED by lineal descendants such as children, grandchildren or their spouses; and it passes under a will or on intestacy.
Residence NRB — who counts

Children include stepchildren, adopted children and foster children. The relief is not available to a person or couple without children. There is NO requirement for the descendants to occupy afterwards, so a sale and distribution of the proceeds does not lose it.
Residence NRB — amount and taper

The LOWER of the net value of the qualifying residence after deducting a mortgage, and the residential enhancement of £175,000. Tapered away at £1 for every £2 by which the net estate exceeds £2m, net value here meaning assets less liabilities but BEFORE reliefs and exemptions.
Residence NRB — transfer and downsizing

The unused percentage transfers between spouses as a brought-forward allowance, capped at 100%, whenever the first spouse died provided the second death was on or after 6 April 2017, and itself tapered if the first estate exceeded £2m. A DOWNSIZING addition restores the lost allowance where the deceased downsized, sold or gave away their home on or after 8 July 2015.

visuals.label: 13.8.2.12 The other death-estate reliefs
rows: Quick-succession relief

Where the deceased's estate had been increased by a chargeable transfer made to them in the 5 YEARS before their death, on which IHT was paid. The percentage starts at 100% and falls by 20% for each full year between the two deaths, and the relief is deducted from the IHT owed AFTER the NRB and residence NRB have been applied. The gifted property need not still be owned at death.
Quick-succession relief — the formula

IHT paid on the first transfer × the QSR percentage × (increase in the donee's estate ÷ that increase plus the IHT paid). So £50,000 tax, 60% and a £200,000 increase gives £50,000 × 60% × (200,000 ÷ 250,000) = £24,000.
Post-mortem relief — quoted shares

Where the PRs sell quoted shares, unit trust units or OEIC shares at a loss within 12 MONTHS of death, a lower value can be substituted. All sales of such investments in the 12-month period are aggregated, profits against losses. It usually produces a repayment of IHT already paid.
Post-mortem relief — land and buildings

The same idea over 3 YEARS from death. Aggregate all profits and losses in the period and deduct any resulting loss from the estate value. Losses on sales in the FOURTH year can also be counted, while profits in the fourth year are ignored.
Woodlands relief

Where the estate includes UK land carrying growing trees and underwood that is not eligible for agricultural or business relief, and the deceased was beneficially entitled for 5 years before death or inherited it on another's death. The value of the woodlands is excluded and the IHT is DEFERRED until they are disposed of. It does not apply to the value of the land itself.

visuals.label: 13.8.2.14 Payment — due date, liability and burden
cols: WHO IS LIABLE AND WHO BEARS IT
rows: Chargeable lifetime transfer, lifetime tax
The LATER of 6 months from the end of the month in which the transfer was made, and 30 April after the tax year in which it was made.

Primary liability on the TRANSFEROR. The transferor may want the trustees to pay out of the trust fund. If the transferor is liable but does not pay, HMRC can pursue the recipients, or in extreme cases the beneficiaries.
CLT, additional tax on death
6 months after the end of the month in which death occurred.

The TRUSTEES are liable, the transferor being dead. The burden falls on the trust fund and so on the beneficiaries. If it is still unpaid 12 months after the end of the month of death, the PRs may become liable.
PET that fails
6 months from the end of the month of the transferor's death.
The RECIPIENT is liable and bears the burden. If unpaid 12 months after the end of the month of death, the PRs become liable.
Death — free estate
6 months after the end of the month in which death occurs.
The PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVES are liable. If the will is silent as to burden it falls on the RESIDUE. Foreign property suffers the IHT attributable to it.
Death — settled property the deceased had an interest in
Same as the death estate.
The TRUSTEES are liable and the burden falls on the trust assets, depleting them for the remaining beneficiaries.
Death — gift with reservation of benefit
Same as the death estate.
The DONEE of the gift is primarily liable for the IHT attributable to the property. If unpaid 12 months after the end of the month of death, the PRs become liable.
Death — property passing outside the will or intestacy
Same as the death estate.
Liability falls on the PRs but the burden is borne by the BENEFICIARY, for example the surviving joint tenant of co-owned property.
Instalment option
First payment on the normal due date, then 10 equal annual amounts.
Claimed with HMRC for certain land and business interests.

visuals.label: 13.8.3 Income tax and CGT during the administration period
rows: The deceased's own tax first

The PRs complete the deceased's income tax return from 6 April to the date of death and settle any income tax owed for that year and any earlier years. This must be finalised BEFORE the IHT liability can be calculated correctly, because tax owed at death is a liability of the estate. The return also includes capital gains in the year of death.
Whose income is it

Income produced by estate assets belongs legally to the PRs until the assets are distributed, so the PRs pay income tax on it. If the PRs sell those assets at a profit, they are liable for CGT instead.
Income tax rates

Non-savings income — trading, rental, employment and pension income — and interest at the basic rate of 20%. From 2026/2027 dividends at the dividend ordinary rate of 10.75%. The personal allowance, personal savings allowance and dividend allowance are NOT available.
Deduction
Where the PRs took out a loan to pay the IHT, interest on that loan is a deductible payment against income.
CGT base cost

PRs are deemed to acquire the deceased's assets at the date of death at market value, the PROBATE VALUE. If a post-mortem relief claim has adjusted the value of quoted shares or land for IHT, that adjusted value becomes the CGT base cost.
CGT rates

From 6 April 2026, 24% for ALL assets, and 32% for carried interest gains. Normal CGT rules apply in computing the gain, and capital losses are set against gains in the same year with any excess carried forward.
Annual exempt amount
Available to PRs for the YEAR OF DEATH AND THE NEXT TWO TAX YEARS ONLY, at the same figure as for individuals — £3,000 for 2024/2025, 2025/2026 and 2026/2027.
Distribution to a beneficiary

Transferring an asset to a beneficiary in satisfaction of a legacy is NOT a disposal for CGT. The beneficiary is deemed to acquire it at the date of death for its probate value, and the value on the day it is actually transferred is irrelevant. The beneficiary's own later disposal compares the proceeds with that probate value.

visuals.label: 13.8.3.3 When the estate need not be reported to HMRC
rows: Income received from 6 April 2024

No need to report if the estate's income from any source is £500 or less. The £500 applies for each tax year of the administration period and cannot be carried over between years, and it covers all types of income except ISAs. If income exceeds £500 you must report ALL of it and cannot deduct the £500.
ISAs
Continue to be exempt from income tax and CGT until the estate is closed, or for up to 3 years after the death.
Income received up to 5 April 2024
No need to report if the only income was bank account interest AND the total tax due on it was £100 or less over the period.
Informal arrangements for a simple estate

Report by writing to HMRC where the estate was valued at less than £2.5 million at the death, the total income tax and CGT due is less than £10,000, and no more than £500,000 of assets was sold in any single tax year of the administration.
Otherwise
Separate returns are required where the administration period spans more than one tax year, and the interest and penalty provisions are the same as for individuals.

visuals.label: 13.8.2.10 Will the relief survive to the donor's death?
rows: The donee retained the property
For business or agricultural relief to be available when calculating tax on the donor's death, the donee must still hold the original property at that date.
Or replaced it within 3 years

Sold and replaced within 3 years with other business or agricultural property, in an ARM'S LENGTH transaction, reinvesting the WHOLE of the net proceeds. All or nothing — there is no partial relief for a partial reinvestment.
No mixing and matching

Business property must be replaced with property qualifying for business relief, and agricultural property with property qualifying for agricultural relief. Within business property the kind may change, so unlisted shares can be replaced by a partnership interest.
Replacement agricultural property

It may still qualify if the original and replacement were occupied by the owner for agriculture for at least 2 years in the 5 years before the death, or owned and occupied for agriculture for at least 7 years in the 10 years before it. Relief is limited to what would have been available before the replacement.
The lifetime calculation is undisturbed
A withdrawal of the relief affects only the tax payable on the donor's death. It does not reopen the original lifetime tax calculation.

notes.head: 13.8.1 How to work any IHT question
body: Take the transfers in order and classify each one: EXEMPT, PET or CLT. Only then think about tax.
For every chargeable transfer, find the nil rate band available by looking back 7 years FROM THAT TRANSFER, using gross figures.
If the donor has died, ask whether any PET has failed, whether taper applies, and whether the reliefs claimed in lifetime survive to the death.
Then do the DEATH ESTATE separately: net assets, no annual exemption, residence NRB before the general NRB, and 40% or 36% on the balance.
Finally, treat the ADMINISTRATION PERIOD as its own tax year or years, with the PRs paying income tax and CGT on what they receive and sell.
The figures, the reliefs, the valuation rules and the payment table are in the collapsed grids above.

notes.head: 13.8.1–13.8.2.4 The shape of inheritance tax
body: Few estates actually pay IHT, because most fall within the nil rate band.

CURRENCY: the NRB and the residence NRB are frozen at £325,000 and £175,000 until APRIL 2031, along with the £2m residence NRB taper threshold. An older note saying the freeze runs to 2028 is out of date.

CURRENCY: leftover private pension pots currently sit OUTSIDE IHT and can pass to beneficiaries tax-free. From APRIL 2027 the unused value of a discretionary private pension will be added to the estate for IHT. That, and the freeze to 2031, will pull more estates over the threshold.
The general rule is that there is no tax on lifetime gifts. IHT is imposed on some of them to stop people transferring property shortly before death and negating the tax altogether.

Transfers to TRUSTS and COMPANIES are always chargeable when made, and may suffer additional tax if the transferor dies within 7 years. Transfers to INDIVIDUALS are not immediately chargeable but become so if the donor dies within 7 years.

CURRENCY: for deaths from 6 APRIL 2025 the connecting factor is LONG-TERM UK RESIDENCE, not domicile. An individual is long-term resident if resident in the UK for at least 10 of the last 20 tax years immediately before the tax year of the chargeable event.
A long-term resident who becomes non-resident stays within scope for a minimum of 3 and a maximum of 10 years, depending on how long they had lived in the UK.

Foreign UNSETTLED property, meaning property owned absolutely rather than on trust, is chargeable if the deceased was a long-term UK resident immediately before the death or transfer, and is EXCLUDED PROPERTY if they were not.
For deaths before 6 April 2025 the old rules applied: deemed UK domicile after residence for 15 of the previous 20 tax years, worldwide assets for the UK domiciled and UK assets only for others.
VALUING a transfer is straightforward for cash, but not for something like stock in a small company, where the value per share depends on the percentage of ownership and so on the control it carries.
Because IHT taxes what the donor gave away, value by the LOSS TO THE DONOR. The worked example is in the decision tree above.

RELATED PROPERTY rules can raise the value: broadly, similar property owned by a spouse or civil partner is taken into account where doing so produces a higher figure. In an assessment the relative stand-alone and related values will be given to you.

notes.head: 13.8.2.5–13.8.2.9 Lifetime transfers, the 7-year rule and taper
body: The three-way classification — exempt, PET or CLT — is worked through in the first decision tree above, and what happens when the donor dies within 7 years is in the second.
The exemptions and their figures are in the collapsed exemptions grid.
IHT is a CUMULATIVE tax. To find the nil rate band available for any chargeable transfer, look back 7 years FROM THAT TRANSFER and deduct the GROSS amounts of earlier chargeable transfers.
Only CLTs use up the nil rate band. PETs are ignored while the donor is alive, and the only reason to think about them at that stage is that they can use up available annual exemptions.

The procedure for lifetime tax on a CLT, in order: identify the value transferred using the loss to donor principle; deduct the annual exemptions to arrive at the CLT; identify the NRB for the year of transfer; deduct other chargeable transfers made in the 7 years before the gift to find the NRB remaining; and charge the excess at 20% or 25%.
TAPER RELIEF reduces the TAX PAYABLE by a percentage. It does not reduce the value of the transfer and it does not give back any nil rate band.
The taper steps are in the second decision tree. Nothing in the first 3 years, then 20%, 40%, 60% and 80% relief across the remaining four.

notes.head: 13.8.2.10 Business relief and agricultural relief
body: CURRENCY: business property relief is now called BUSINESS RELIEF. The Business examinable-law update confirms the change of name at 7.20.
CURRENCY: from 6 APRIL 2026 a COMBINED £2.5m cap applies to 100% relief across business and agricultural property. Value above the cap attracts 50% relief.
Any unused allowance is transferable between spouses, so a couple can pass on up to £5m of business or agricultural assets, on top of the NRB and residence NRB.
Both reliefs reduce the value transferred and are given BEFORE any annual exemption.
The rates and the qualifying assets are in the mind map above. The two conditions that decide most questions are the TRADING requirement and the OWNERSHIP period.

TRADING: relief is given only if the business is trading. A business that holds or makes investments, or deals in property, is excluded. A company acquiring land for rental income or to sell on after it appreciates is dealing in land and gets nothing.
Shares in OVERSEAS trading companies are eligible for business relief.

OWNERSHIP: the donor must generally have owned the business property for at least 2 years before the transfer. Exceptions include replacing one business asset with another within a 3-year period, and inheriting business property from a spouse.

EXCEPTED ASSETS make the relief proportional. An excepted asset is one neither used wholly or mainly for the purposes of the business throughout the 2 years before the transfer, nor required for future use in it [IHTA 1984 s 112(2)].
Typical examples are investments, assets held for the transferor's personal use, and large cash deposits not needed by the business. If 30% of the company's assets are excepted, relief drops to 70%.

AGRICULTURAL PROPERTY means agricultural land or buildings used for agriculture and situated in the UK. Relief is available both to a farmer who owns and uses the land, and to a landowner letting it to a farmer — there is no requirement to farm it yourself.
EXCLUDED from agriculture: grazing horses, except in connection with a stud farm, and land used for fishing, shooting and other sporting rights.
AGRICULTURAL VALUE, not market or development value, is what the relief covers — the value assuming the land can be used only for farming and any development is prohibited.

AGRICULTURAL OCCUPATION: 2 years' occupation by the transferor for the purposes of agriculture, extended to 7 YEARS where the land is TENANTED, that is let to someone else who occupies it for agriculture.
The two reliefs can apply to the SAME transfer. Agricultural relief is given first, on the farmland and buildings.

Business relief then covers the assets used in the farming business that are not agricultural land or buildings, such as plant, machinery and goodwill — and can also pick up DEVELOPMENT VALUE within the land that agricultural relief cannot reach.

On a lifetime transfer the reliefs have immediate effect only for CLTs, because PETs are not immediately chargeable. Whether they survive to be used on the death is the last node of the second decision tree above.

notes.head: 13.8.2.11–13.8.2.12 The death estate
body: At death the deceased is treated as having made a chargeable transfer equal to the NET value of their assets — total value less debts and liabilities owed at the date of death. The personal representatives pay the tax on it.
The calculation mirrors death tax on lifetime transfers, with one difference: the ANNUAL EXEMPTION is not available to reduce the chargeable death estate.

Start with the NRB for the year of death and reduce it by chargeable transfers — failed PETs and CLTs — made in the 7 years before death. The remainder is deducted from the estate and the balance is taxed at 40%.
In practice PETs and CLTs in the 7 years before death often use the whole band, so the entire death estate is charged at 40%.
Gifts on death to a SPOUSE or civil partner and to a CHARITY are exempt, with the same £325,000 restriction where the deceased was UK domiciled and the recipient spouse was not.
CURRENCY: from April 2024, gifts on death to European Economic Area charities are no longer exempt.

The REDUCED RATE of 36% applies where 10% or more of the deceased's NET estate is left to charity. The baseline amount is the estate charged to IHT after all reliefs, exemptions and the available NRB, but EXCLUDING the charitable legacy itself, and IGNORING the residence NRB.

The ESTATE RATE is the average rate of tax applicable to each item of property in the estate. Where the NRB was completely used by lifetime transfers the estate rate is 40%, unless the 36% rate applies.
Valuation rules, the two nil rate bands, and the further reliefs — quick succession, post-mortem and woodlands — are in the collapsed grids above.

notes.head: 13.8.2.13–13.8.2.15 Anti-avoidance and tax planning
body: GIFTS WITH RESERVATION OF BENEFIT stop a donor giving an asset away while continuing to derive benefit from it. If they do, the asset is treated as still forming part of their estate at death. The classic case is giving away the house and continuing to live in it rent-free.
The asset is brought back in at its value AT DEATH, not its value when given. A house given away at £400,000 and worth £600,000 at the death comes back in at £600,000.
The rules do NOT apply where the donor pays MARKET RENT for continued occupation, or in situations where HMRC guidance treats the remaining benefit as insignificant.

RELEASING the reservation before death avoids the rules, because the asset is only brought back if a benefit is retained AT the date of death. But to stop death-bed releases, HMRC treats the release as a PET at the date of release, valued at the asset's value then.
DOUBLE CHARGES RELIEF prevents a double charge, for instance where the original gift was a PET, the donor died within 7 years, and they were still living in the house.
HMRC computes the tax on the PET alone and on the gift with reservation alone, and charges whichever produces the higher figure — usually taxing the house in the death estate and ignoring the PET.

PRE-OWNED ASSET TAX catches what the reservation rules miss, for example selling a house, giving the cash proceeds away, and living rent-free in the property the donee then buys. It imposes an INCOME TAX charge where the former owner benefits directly or indirectly from an asset they previously owned and the transfer is not within the gifts with reservation rules.

TAX PLANNING: make lifetime gifts, because a PET where the donor survives 7 years escapes IHT entirely, and even a failed PET is tapered. APPRECIATING assets are the ones to give away, because it is the value at the DATE OF TRANSFER that counts, not the value at death.

Also: use the £3,000 annual exemption every year and the other exemptions where relevant; use any transferable NRBs from a previous marriage, which are otherwise wasted; invest in business or agricultural property, which attract relief of up to 100% while still being passed on; and make sure the will itself is tax efficient.

notes.head: 13.8.3 Taxation of the estate in administration
body: The PRs must deal with HMRC and settle all tax liabilities arising from the death, and on the income and gains made during the administration period.
The order matters: finalise the DECEASED'S income tax and capital gains to the date of death FIRST, because any tax owed at death is a liability of the estate and so affects the IHT calculation.
The PRs' own income tax and CGT during the administration, the rates, the annual exempt amount and the treatment of distributions to beneficiaries are in the collapsed grid above.

CURRENCY: the PR CGT rate is 24% for ALL assets from 6 April 2026, with 32% for carried interest gains. The old split between 20% for general assets and a higher rate for residential property no longer applies.
CURRENCY: the annual exempt amount is available to PRs for the year of death AND THE NEXT TWO TAX YEARS. A note saying it is nil in every year after death is wrong.
CURRENCY: from 2026/2027 dividends received by PRs are charged at the dividend ordinary rate of 10.75%.
There is no CGT on the death itself. CGT arises only on the PRs' own disposals, and later on a beneficiary's disposal of what they inherited.
The reporting thresholds, including the £500 de minimis and the informal arrangements for simple estates, are in the collapsed grid above.

statutes.text: A disposition is not a transfer of value if it is shown that it was not intended, and was not made in a transaction intended, to confer any gratuitous benefit on any person, and either it was made in a transaction at arm's length between persons not connected with each other, or it was such as might be expected to be made in such a transaction.
Expenditure on the maintenance of an individual's family, such as paying a child's school fees, is not treated as a transfer of value for IHT, even though the donor's estate is reduced by it.

Defines the POTENTIALLY EXEMPT TRANSFER: a lifetime transfer of value by an individual to another individual which is neither exempt nor immediately chargeable. It is treated as exempt while the donor lives and becomes a chargeable transfer only if the donor dies within 7 years.

TAPER RELIEF. Where a chargeable transfer was made more than 3 years before the death, the tax charged on it is reduced: by 20% for 3 to 4 years, 40% for 4 to 5, 60% for 5 to 6 and 80% for 6 to 7. It reduces the TAX, not the value of the transfer, and does not restore nil rate band.

TRANSFERABLE NIL RATE BAND. Where a person dies leaving all or part of their nil rate band unused, a claim may be made on the death of their surviving spouse or civil partner to increase that survivor's band by the unused PERCENTAGE, applied to the band in force at the second death. The maximum uplift is 100%, so the survivor can have at most two full bands.

RESIDENCE NIL RATE BAND. An additional band, currently £175,000, where the estate includes a qualifying residential interest closely inherited by lineal descendants. It applies to the death estate only, is deducted before the general nil rate band, and is tapered away at £1 for every £2 by which the net estate exceeds £2m.

Defines RELEVANT BUSINESS PROPERTY for business relief, and the categories attracting 100% and 50% relief. Relief is given only where the business is TRADING; a business consisting wholly or mainly of dealing in securities, stocks or shares, land or buildings, or of making or holding investments, does not qualify.

EXCEPTED ASSETS. An asset is excepted, and so excluded from business relief, if it was neither used wholly or mainly for the purposes of the business throughout the 2 years immediately preceding the transfer, nor required at the time of the transfer for future use in the business. Relief is then given proportionally.

AGRICULTURAL RELIEF. Reduces the AGRICULTURAL VALUE of agricultural property in the UK. The property must have been occupied by the transferor for the purposes of agriculture throughout the 2 years before the transfer, or owned by them and occupied for agriculture throughout the 7 years before it where the land is tenanted.

QUICK-SUCCESSION RELIEF. Where the value of a person's estate was increased by a chargeable transfer made to them within the 5 years before their death, the tax on their death is reduced. The percentage is 100% falling by 20% for each full year between the two events.

Section 160 sets the general valuation rule: the price the property might reasonably be expected to fetch if sold in the open market at that time. Section 161 contains the RELATED PROPERTY rules, under which property owned by a spouse or civil partner is taken into account where that produces a higher value.

THE INSTALMENT OPTION. Tax attributable to certain property, including land and business interests, may on election be paid in 10 equal yearly instalments, the first falling due on the normal due date.

GIFTS WITH RESERVATION OF BENEFIT. Where an individual disposes of property by gift but possession and enjoyment is not bona fide assumed by the donee, or the property is not enjoyed to the entire exclusion of the donor, the property is treated as still forming part of the donor's estate on death, valued at that date.

PRE-OWNED ASSET TAX. Imposes an INCOME TAX charge on the benefit received by the former owner of property where they continue to benefit directly or indirectly from an asset they previously owned and the gifts with reservation rules do not apply.

On a death, the assets of which the deceased was competent to dispose are deemed to be acquired by the personal representatives at their market value at the date of death, but are NOT deemed to be disposed of by the deceased. So there is no CGT on death itself, and the PROBATE VALUE becomes the base cost. A transfer to a legatee is likewise not a disposal by the PRs.

13.8.tip: ⚡ 13.8 SPINE — three taxes, taken in turn. For IHT, classify every lifetime gift as EXEMPT, PET or CLT, cumulate seven years back FROM THE GIFT on gross figures, then value the death estate by LOSS TO THE DONOR. Take the reliefs before the bands: business and agricultural relief first, then the RNRB, then the NRB. Taper reduces the TAX and never the transfer. Deaths from 6 April 2025 turn on LONG-TERM UK RESIDENCE rather than domicile, and the bands are frozen to April 2031. Then deal with the estate's own income tax and CGT: settle the deceased's tax first, remember the PRs get no allowances, and note that death itself is not a disposal.
